sources.title: Nicolas Libedinsky and Geordie Williamson, The anti-spherical category (author-hosted complete PDF of the article)
sources.locator: Sections 1.1-1.3 (printed pp. 1-4) and Sections 2.1-2.7 (printed pp. 6-9): the anti-spherical module sgn_v (x)_{H_I} H, the Hecke normalization (h_s+v)(h_s-v^-1)=0, standard and canonical bases, the parabolic property (2.3), the spherical and anti-spherical modules with their standard bases and right action formulas (2.4)-(2.6), the bar compatibility (2.7) and Theorem 2.2(2)-(3), and the relations (1)-(3) of 2.7 (Deodhar's alternating sum n_{y,x}=sum (-v)^{l(z)}h_{zy,x} and the spherical reduction m_{y,x}=h_{w_0 y,w_0 x}); the complete sections were read in the retrieved full text.

contents.name: Section 2.4: definition of the spherical module M = L(v^-1) (x)_{H_I} H and the anti-spherical module N = L(-v) (x)_{H_I} H, with standard bases over the minimal coset representatives ^IW
Sections 2.5-2.6: right action formulas (2.5)-(2.6) of C_s=b_s=H_s+v, the bar compatibility (2.7), and Theorem 2.2(2)-(3) existence and uniqueness of the self-dual bases c_x, d_x
Section 2.7(1)-(2): the families m_{y,x}, n_{y,x} for y,x in ^IW, the dictionary to Deodhar's polynomials in the cases u=-1 and u=q, and the spherical reduction m_{y,x}=h_{w0 y,w0 x} for finitary W_I
Section 2.7(3): Deodhar's alternating-sum formula n_{y,x}=sum_{z in W_I}(-v)^{l(z)}h_{zy,x}
Sections 1.1-1.2 and 5-6: positivity of sign parabolic Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials and the diagrammatic categorification of the anti-spherical module
contents.reason: The page uses the triangular-induction construction of the canonical bases already available locally from the published Kazhdan-Lusztig basis theorem; the Hecke-category and light-leaves machinery is a categorification topic of another frontier and is not needed for the multiplicity theorems.

contents.name: Section 2.3: the parabolic property (2.3), x in ^IW and xs not in ^IW implies xs=rx with r in I

sources.locator: Sections 1-3 (printed pp. 1-7) of the complete 7-page lecture: standard filtrations (Theorem-Definition 1.1, Corollary 1.3, Lemma 1.10), BGG reciprocity (Theorem 2.2), translation functors (Constructions 3.1-3.7, Lemmas 3.2-3.5), facets and upper closures (Definitions 3.8-3.9, Example 3.11), Theorem 3.12 with its proof sketch, Theorem 3.13, Remark 3.14, Example 3.16, Construction 3.17 and Exercise 3.18; the complete lecture text was read in the retrieved full text.

contents.name: Theorem-Definition 1.1 and Corollary 1.3: standard (Verma) filtrations characterised by Ext-vanishing against dual Vermas
Theorem 2.2: BGG reciprocity (P_mu : M_lambda) = [M_lambda : L_mu]
Lemma 3.3 and Construction 3.7: exactness and biadjunction of the translation functors, including L(nu)* as adjoint
Lemma 3.5: the tensor E (x) M_lambda has a standard filtration with multiplicities dim E_{mu-lambda}
Theorem 3.12(1): (T_lambda^mu)(M_{w.lambda}) = M_{w.mu} for all w
Theorem 3.12(2): (T_lambda^mu)(L_{w.lambda}) is L_{w.mu} if F_{w.mu} is contained in F^+_{w.lambda} and 0 otherwise
Construction 3.17 and Exercise 3.18: the big projective Xi_mu = T_{-rho}^mu(L_{-rho}) is projective and injective, has all standard multiplicities 1 and equals P_mu
Example 3.16: the sl_2 computation sending L_{-2} to L_{-1} and L_0 to 0
Theorem 3.13: equal facets give an equivalence of blocks
contents.reason: The equal-facet equivalence is stronger than the numerical transport and is not consumed by this page; the analogous regular-block numerical transport is a scaffolded item of the sibling batch 14 and no item here depends on the equivalence.
